stimulus.title: Urban Beekeeping
stimulus.html:
A Over the past two decades, beekeeping has moved from the countryside to the rooftops of large cities. In London alone, the number of registered hives more than doubled between 2008 and 2018, and similar growth has been reported in Paris, Berlin and New York. Many of the new beekeepers are office workers who see the hobby as a way to reconnect with nature.

B Supporters argue that city bees enjoy several advantages. Urban gardens, parks and balconies offer a wide variety of flowers, and because pesticides are used less often in cities than on farms, the bees may be exposed to fewer harmful chemicals. Some studies have even found that honey produced in cities contains a greater mix of pollen types than honey from rural areas.

C However, not all scientists are convinced that the trend is beneficial. Honeybees compete with wild bees for the same flowers, and in areas where hives are densely packed, there may simply not be enough food to go around. A 2019 survey in one European capital found that the amount of pollen and nectar available per hive had fallen sharply as new colonies were added.

D For this reason, several conservation groups now encourage city residents to plant more flowering species rather than install new hives. They point out that a single window box filled with lavender or thyme can support dozens of wild insects.

stimulus.title: The Humble Pencil
stimulus.html:
A For a tool that most people use without a second thought, the pencil has a surprisingly long history. Before pencils existed, writers in ancient Rome used a thin metal rod called a stylus, often made of lead, to leave light marks on papyrus. This is why the writing core of a pencil is still called "lead" in English, even though modern pencils contain no lead at all.

B The story of the modern pencil began in the 1560s, when a large deposit of graphite was discovered near Borrowdale in northern England. Local shepherds first used the soft black material to mark their sheep. Graphite left a darker line than lead and was easy to remove, so it soon became popular with artists. Because graphite breaks easily, people began wrapping sticks of it in string or sheepskin to hold it.

C The Borrowdale graphite was so valuable that the mine was guarded, and at times it was deliberately flooded to prevent theft. England had what was effectively a monopoly on pencil production for almost two hundred years, as the graphite found elsewhere in Europe was of poorer quality and crumbled when it was cut into sticks.

D A solution came from France. In 1795, during a war that cut France off from English supplies, an army officer named Nicolas-Jacques Conté developed a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and baking the mixture in a kiln. By changing the proportion of clay, he could make pencils that were harder or softer. This process is still used today, and it is the reason pencils are graded with letters such as H for hard and B for black.

E Pencils were originally sold unpainted, to show off the quality of the wood. In the 1890s, however, some manufacturers began painting their pencils yellow. At the time, the best graphite came from China, and yellow was associated with Chinese royalty. The colour suggested luxury and quality, and in North America it remains the most common colour for pencils today.

F Although digital devices have replaced pencils for many purposes, around fourteen billion pencils are still produced every year. Pencils work in extreme cold and in zero gravity, and astronauts have taken them on space missions. They are also cheap, and their marks can easily be erased, an advantage that no pen has ever fully matched.

stimulus.title: Sleep and Memory
stimulus.html:
A For most of the twentieth century, scientists regarded sleep as a passive state, a period in which the brain simply switched off to rest. That view has changed dramatically. Researchers now believe that sleep plays an active role in learning, and in particular in consolidation, the process by which new memories become stable and long-lasting.

B Some of the earliest evidence came from a simple experiment in 1924. Two American psychologists, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach, asked students to learn lists of nonsense syllables and then tested them either after a period of sleep or after the same period awake. The students remembered far more after sleeping. At the time, the researchers concluded that sleep merely protected memories from interference by new information. It was not until much later that scientists suspected sleep might strengthen memories directly.

C Modern studies suggest how this happens. During deep sleep, the hippocampus, a region involved in forming new memories, appears to "replay" patterns of activity recorded during the day. In experiments with rats, scientists have observed the sequence of nerve-cell activity produced as the animals ran through a maze being repeated, at higher speed, while they slept. This replay is thought to help transfer information to the cortex, where long-term memories are stored.

D Different stages of sleep may support different kinds of memory. Deep, slow-wave sleep seems particularly important for facts and events, while rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most dreaming occurs, may matter more for skills and emotional memories. In one study, people who were trained in a new motor task, typing a sequence of keys, improved by about twenty percent after a night's sleep, without any further practice.

E These findings have practical implications, especially for students. Staying up all night before an exam may be one of the least effective ways to prepare. Research shows that a single night without sleep can reduce the ability to form new memories by as much as forty percent. Even a daytime nap of sixty to ninety minutes, if it includes deep sleep, can improve performance on memory tests.

F Not all questions have been answered, however. Scientists still disagree about why we dream, and whether dreams themselves play any part in memory. Some argue that dreams are simply a side effect of the brain's activity during REM sleep. Others believe that dreams allow us to rehearse difficult situations safely. As measurement techniques improve, researchers hope to settle these debates.

stimulus.title: Is Four the New Five?
stimulus.html:
A The idea that people should work five days a week is less than a century old. In 1926, the American car maker Henry Ford introduced a five-day, forty-hour week in his factories, arguing that workers with more free time would buy more products. Today, a growing number of companies are asking whether the time has come for another reduction.

B The best-known recent experiment took place in the United Kingdom in 2022, when around sixty companies allowed their staff to work four days a week for six months without any cut in pay. The trial was organised by a non-profit group and studied by researchers from several universities. At the end, most of the companies chose to continue with the shorter week, and staff reported lower levels of stress and fewer sick days.

C Supporters argue that the benefits go beyond happier employees. Economist Laura Mendez points out that when people have less time, they tend to cut unnecessary meetings and focus on the tasks that matter. "Many office workers are only truly productive for a few hours a day," she says. "A shorter week forces organisations to remove waste." Psychologist Tom Erikson adds that the extra day off gives people time for exercise and family, which in turn improves their concentration at work.

D Critics, however, warn that the model does not suit every industry. Hospitals, schools and shops cannot simply close for an extra day, and covering the missing hours would require hiring more staff. Business consultant Priya Shah argues that the trials so far have mainly involved small office-based firms that chose to take part, so the results may not apply to the wider economy. "Companies that volunteer for an experiment like this are usually the ones that expect it to work," she says.

E There are also different ways of reducing working time. Some companies give everyone the same day off, usually Friday. Others stagger days off so that the business stays open five days a week. A few have tried a "compressed" week, in which employees work the same number of hours in four longer days, but Mendez says this approach often leads to tiredness and loses many of the benefits.

F In my view, the evidence so far is encouraging but incomplete. It would be a mistake for governments to force a four-day week on all employers. However, the trials suggest that many organisations could reduce working hours without harming their results, and for them, the experiment is clearly worth trying.

stimulus.title: Counting Without Words
stimulus.html:
A In the early twentieth century, a horse in Berlin named Clever Hans became famous for apparently solving arithmetic problems. Asked to add five and three, Hans would tap his hoof eight times. Crowds were astonished, and a panel of experts initially found no evidence of trickery. It was the psychologist Oskar Pfungst who eventually showed that Hans could not count at all. Instead, the horse was reacting to tiny, unconscious changes in the posture and facial expression of his questioner, who relaxed slightly when the correct number of taps was reached. When Hans could not see anyone who knew the answer, his performance collapsed.

B The case of Clever Hans made scientists deeply suspicious of claims about animal intelligence, and for decades the idea that animals might understand numbers was treated with caution. Yet carefully controlled experiments over the past fifty years have shown that many species possess what researchers call a "number sense": an ability to judge quantities without language or symbols.

C Much of this ability is approximate. When monkeys, fish or young children are asked to choose the larger of two groups of dots, their accuracy depends not on the absolute difference between the groups but on their ratio. Distinguishing eight dots from sixteen is easy; distinguishing fifteen from sixteen is very hard, even though the second pair differs by only one. This pattern, known as Weber's law, appears across a remarkable range of animals, which suggests that the underlying mechanism evolved long ago.

D Some animals, however, appear capable of more precise judgements with small numbers. In a well-known series of studies, the psychologist Irene Pepperberg trained an African grey parrot named Alex to say the number of objects on a tray, up to six. Alex could also answer questions such as "How many green blocks?" when the tray held blocks of several colours. Critics pointed out that Alex had received thousands of hours of training and argued that his abilities told us little about parrots in the wild. Pepperberg accepted that the training was unusual but maintained that it revealed abilities which the bird's brain must already have possessed.

E Why would animals need a sense of number at all? In the wild, the answer is often survival. Lions approaching a rival group appear to compare the number of roars they hear with the number of lions in their own group before deciding whether to attack. Bees can be trained to fly past a set number of landmarks to find food. And the females of some frog species choose mates according to the number of pulses in a male's call, since a longer call suggests a stronger male.

F Perhaps the most surprising recent evidence comes from insects. In 2018, researchers in Australia reported that honeybees could learn the concept of zero, understanding that an empty set is smaller than a set containing one item. Since bees have fewer than a million brain cells, compared with around eighty-six billion in humans, the finding suggests that numerical abilities may not require a large brain. Some researchers remain cautious, noting that the bees might have been responding to other features of the images, such as the total area covered by shapes. The authors, however, say they controlled for such factors.

G What does all this mean for human mathematics? Most researchers agree that our approximate number sense is inherited from our animal ancestors. What appears to be uniquely human is the use of symbols, words and written numerals, that allow us to represent exact quantities of any size. Without such symbols, even humans struggle: studies of communities whose languages have no words for numbers above three or four have found that adults find it difficult to match exact quantities larger than that.
